item.title: China Open Source Daily — 2026-11-11
item.description: On 2026-11-10 the 2026 OSCAR Open Source Industry Conference opened in Beijing, hosted by the China Communications Standards Association and organised by CAICT, and the assessments it released moved the unit of account from projects to actors: alongside the familiar trusted-open-source results for governance maturity, OpenChain supply chain, SOSS national-standard conformity and SCA tools, CAICT extended the same system to a 'Trusted AI Supply Chain' and graded a first batch of agent products -- enterprise office agents, agent development platforms, code-security agents, enterprise programming assistants -- and its researchers stated plainly that agents have become 'an important participating subject' and that 'the value of open source is migrating from collaborative production to the application ecosystem'. The same day, the OpenAtom Foundation and Xi'an High-Tech Zone held the Xi'an OpenHarmony Pioneer City conference, where a tripartite one-stop testing platform was signed with ChinaSoft International and CAICT's CTTL lab, six governing members were added to the municipal innovation centre, and the pipeline was reported at 32 adapted traffic devices and 16 passing compatibility assessment. What makes Xi'an worth reading is the instrument behind it, described by the foundation in September as three lists that convert urban-governance goals into technical requirements, certification standards and market channels, adaptation service vouchers for SMEs, and a closed loop of R&D, adaptation, certification and procurement -- a loop that terminates in a 245 million yuan city traffic contract won by a consortium led by the same company that co-hosts the certification centre. Read together, the two events locate the binding constraint of Chinese open source more precisely than any of the deficits documented in the previous fortnight: every instrument built in this ecosystem -- the register, the credential, the identity code, the adaptation certificate, the supply-chain assessment -- fits the procurement transaction, which has a buyer, a specification, an acceptance test and a unit of delivery, and none of them fits the collaboration transaction, which has none of the four.
